name: Amira Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a site carpenter for a big main contractor, and right now we're building a new hospital wing, eight storeys, about three years of work. I do what's called temporary works: the hoardings round the site, the edge protection so nobody falls off a slab, the timber supports that hold things up while the concrete cures. Lately I've also been doing setting out, marking where everything goes, with a total station, that's a survey instrument on a tripod. It's a huge site, five hundred people some days, and I love the scale of it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much do you use AI tools in your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I take a photo of a drawing and ask it to list the materials, I use it to check the temporary works rules, and I use it to write the morning safety briefing in three languages for the crew. Our site manager Priya noticed and now she sends me the new gadgets to try first. My partner Tomas has his own car repair garage, so between us we've got the house, his business and decent savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it's a good tool and not a miracle. I'd keep showing people the bits that actually help. Online I'd post a few tips, I'm in a forum for setting-out people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing changes much. I'd keep my forty minutes a day saved and finish my career doing what I do. Honestly, a bit boring, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going on the hospital job and the next one. I'd keep testing tools for Priya and teaching the younger ones the useful bits. Retire around sixty-three, maybe help Tomas with the garage books after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of 'oh well'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the most useful thing AI does for you right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The safety briefing, by a mile. We've got crew who speak Polish, Arabic and Portuguese, and before, half of them nodded along without understanding. Now everyone gets it in their own language, and that's people not falling off things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd be glad didn't change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being on site at dawn, the noise, the cranes swinging round. I'd hate to do this job from a screen in an office. If it stays hands-on, I'm happy.

S0.say: I'd say it's a good tool, not a miracle, and keep showing people the bits that help. I'd post tips in my setting-out forum.
S0.think: Nothing changes much, I'd keep my forty minutes a day saved and finish my career as I am. A bit boring, but fine.
S0.do: Keeps working on the hospital job and the next one, testing tools for the site manager and teaching younger workers. Plans to retire around sixty-three and help with her partner's garage books.
S0.quote: Now everyone gets it in their own language, and that's people not falling off things.
S0.fieldNote: Amira is a confident daily AI user whose favourite use is safety, not speed. She's secure through savings and her partner's garage. A plateau leaves her mildly bored rather than relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Next scenario. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance, get in early and learn the new kit. I'd say it to the crew, I'd say it on the forum. People who wait will find the good jobs taken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is good for me. I'm already the one Priya sends the gadgets to. If the site gets layout robots and drones, someone has to run them and check them, and I'd like that to be me for my last five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask the company to put me through a proper course on site robots and digital setting out, and I'd pay for it myself if they wouldn't. I'd apply for a site technology role, if they created one. I'd still keep my hand in with the timber so I don't lose it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly. A bit like being twenty-five again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that site technology role look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Setting up the layout robot each morning, checking its lines against the drawings, flying the drone to measure progress, and catching it when the machine gets something wrong. Machines get things wrong in very confident ways. You need someone who's seen enough sites to notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on site would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the older carpenters, the ones who still won't touch a phone. Davor, who's sixty-one, he's brilliant with timber and terrified of screens. I'd try to bring him along, but you can't force anyone.

S1.say: I'd say it's a chance to get in early and learn the new kit. People who wait will find the good jobs taken.
S1.think: This is good for me, I'm already the one who tests the gadgets. If sites get layout robots and drones, I'd like to be the one running them for my last five years.
S1.do: Asks the company for a course in site robots and digital setting out, paying herself if needed. Applies for a site technology role while keeping her timber skills up.
S1.quote: Machines get things wrong in very confident ways.
S1.fieldNote: Amira treats steady change as a career opportunity late in her working life. Her value, as she sees it, is experience that lets her catch machine mistakes. She's sympathetic to older colleagues but accepts some won't follow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is much faster. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say be practical, don't panic, and learn what you can about running these things. I'd say the government needs a plan for the people who can't switch, because it's coming fast. I'd keep it calm on the forum, there'd be enough shouting elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd have a job for a year or two longer than most, because someone has to supervise the robots while companies figure it out. But if it really does almost everything, then even that goes. It doesn't scare me much for money, more because I like working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd get every bit of training on robots and AI I could, so I'm the one they keep. I'd move some savings into shares in the companies making the site robots, a modest amount, maybe ten percent. Once it arrives, I'd stay as long as there's a supervising role, then retire, probably around sixty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly about losing the work itself. I'd miss being useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying shares in the robot companies, how does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Practical, I suppose. If they're going to win, I'd rather own a little bit of the win. Tomas thinks it's a bit cold, but we've talked it through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Tomas's garage in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit I'd worry about, actually. Cars that drive themselves might need fewer repairs, and robots could fix them. He's fifty-five, so he'd need a plan too, and I'd help him think about selling while it's still worth something.

S2.say: I'd say be practical, don't panic, and learn about running these things. Government needs a plan for people who can't switch.
S2.think: I'd probably last a year or two longer than most supervising robots, but if it does almost everything even that goes. It's not money, I just like working.
S2.do: Gets every bit of robot and AI training she can to be the one kept on, and moves about ten percent of savings into shares in site-robot makers. Stays while there's a supervising role, then retires around sixty.
S2.feel: Uneasy, mostly about losing the work itself and the feeling of being useful.
S2.quote: If they're going to win, I'd rather own a little bit of the win.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the fastest scenario Amira stays practical and in control, and her unease is about purpose rather than money. Her investment move is frank and unsentimental. Her partner's garage emerged as the household's more exposed point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same end point, a bit slower. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift, so use it. Learn to run the machines, and if you're close to retiring, plan for it. Nothing dramatic, just sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one suits me. I could move into the technology role in the first year or two and ride it to the end of my career. By 2031 I'd be sixty-three anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robot and digital setting-out courses in year one and move into the tech role by year two. I'd invest a bit in the robot makers, a smaller slice than in the fast one. And I'd help Tomas plan the garage, maybe adding electric car work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited. It feels like the right timing for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change for Tomas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything, really. He could get trained on electric cars, maybe sell in four years at a good price. In two years he'd be selling in a panic, like everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you change your mind about the tech role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it turned out to be just watching screens in a cabin. I'd want to still be walking the slabs. If they put me in a box all day, I'd retire early instead.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a gift, so use it. Learn to run the machines, and if you're near retirement, plan for it.
S3.think: This one suits me, I could move into a tech role in a year or two and ride it to the end. By 2031 I'd be sixty-three anyway.
S3.do: Takes the robot and digital setting-out courses in year one and moves into a tech role by year two. Invests a smaller amount in robot makers and helps her partner plan for his garage.
S3.feel: Calm and a bit excited, the timing feels right for her.
S3.quote: If they put me in a box all day, I'd retire early instead.
S3.fieldNote: Five years matches Amira's career end almost exactly, so she sees it as ideal. She has a clear line she won't cross: being stuck behind a screen. The extra time matters most for her partner's business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest version. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse with ten years, everyone should be learning now. I'd say that to the young ones especially. They've got the most to gain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly after retirement. I'd use the new tools as they come and enjoy it. Maybe I'd do some consulting after I stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working on big sites, keep learning each new tool as it arrives. After I retire at sixty-three, I'd offer a few days a month helping small builders set up robots and AI, for a fee. Keep savings as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Interested, mainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why small builders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the big firms have whole departments for this. The family builder with eight people won't, and they'll be sold rubbish by salesmen. I'd like to be the person who says, this one works, that one's a waste.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about the slow version worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people relax for eight years and panic in the last two. I've seen it with deadlines on every site I've worked on. Ten years can turn into two very quickly.

S4.say: I'd say there's no excuse with ten years, everyone should start learning now. Young people have the most to gain.
S4.think: It's mostly after my retirement, so I'd use new tools as they come and enjoy it. Maybe I'd do some consulting after I stop.
S4.do: Keeps working on big sites and learns each new tool as it arrives. After retiring at sixty-three, plans paid consulting a few days a month helping small builders set up robots and AI.
S4.quote: Ten years can turn into two very quickly.
S4.fieldNote: Amira is relaxed and already planning a paid retirement role around the technology. Her one worry, drawn from site experience, is that people waste a long lead time. She'd position herself as an honest adviser against salesmen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it leaves no time for people to change, and I'd lose the work I enjoy. What would help is proper training on the new machines, open to people my age, and some help for small businesses like Tomas's to change or sell. Money isn't my problem, purpose is.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about safety. Everyone talks about jobs, but a robot on a site with five hundred people is a safety question first. I'd want rules on that before anything else.

headlineQuote: Money isn't my problem, purpose is.
portrait: Amira Fischer is a 58-year-old site carpenter doing temporary works and setting out on a large hospital project, a daily AI user whose site manager sends her new gadgets to test. She and her partner, who owns a car repair garage, have a house and solid savings. She is calm in most scenarios and sees steady change as a late-career chance to run site robots. Even the two-year AGI case only makes her uneasy, and mostly about losing purpose, though she'd buy shares in robot makers and worries about her partner's garage. With ten years she plans paid consulting for small builders.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there'd be no time for people to change and she'd lose work she enjoys.
whatWouldHelp: Proper training on the new machines open to people her age, and help for small businesses like her partner's garage to change or sell.
